Within the section on "Explanation" (Jieshi-fen), there are two parts: first, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one;

second, the actual explanation. 1. Concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one: Having already explained the section on "Establishing the Meaning" (Liyi-fen), the section on "Explanation" is now explained. 2. The actual explanation. [The explanation follows...]
The text contains three parts:
first, the indication of the number;
second, the enumeration of the names.
Third, the analysis of characteristics.
There are three types of explanation; what are these three? First, the demonstration of the correct meaning. Within the listing of names, first is the demonstration of the correct meaning.
This correctly explains the established Mahāyāna doctrine.
Second, it serves as an antidote to erroneous attachments; once correct reasoning is clarified, emotional delusions are thereby dispelled.
Therefore, there is the counteractive measure against false attachments.

Third is the discernment of the characteristics of setting out upon the path: once false attachments have been eliminated, one next distinguishes the successive stages of ascending toward the correct path.
Therefore, there is the characteristic of the analytical entry into the path.
Within the "Discernment of Characteristics," the explanation of the aforementioned three names constitutes three sections.
The beginning and middle have two parts:
first, the general;
second, the specific.
"Summary" refers to the explanation of the passage in the "Section on Establishing the Thesis" concerning how the minds of sentient beings encompass all things, and so forth.
"Distinction" refers to the specific meanings of the two sections following "For what reason? within the aforementioned section on the Establishment of the Thesis.
This section as a whole contains three parts.
First, opening the gate according to the Dharma;
second, enumerating its two gates;
third, the comprehensive inclusion within these two gates.

The Manifestation of the True Principle states that based on the Dharma of the One Mind, there are two gates. What are these two? First, the gate of the true suchness of mind; second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind. Regarding the first of these, "One Mind" is said as follows:
That is to say, the single *tathāgatagarbha*-mind contains two meanings.
First, the meaning of being devoid of characteristics with respect to its essence;
this is the gate of *tathatā* (suchness).
That is to say: it is neither defiled nor pure;
neither arising nor ceasing;
unmoving and non-turning.
Equal and of one flavor,
its nature is without differentiation;
sentient beings are themselves nirvāṇa.
It does not depend on extinction.
Ordinary beings and Maitreya share the same limit.
These two follow the principle of arising and ceasing according to conditions.
This is precisely the gate of arising and ceasing.

It means that, following the influence of perfuming, movement arises, resulting in either defilement or purity. Although defilement and purity are thus established, [the fundamental nature remains unchanged].
The nature is eternally unmoving;
yet it is precisely through this immobility that defilement and purity are established.
Therefore, immobility is also included within the category of movement.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states that consciousness has two meanings, among which original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) is one;
the preceding passage within the section on arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*) identifies its own essence as the other.
As stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
"Being unstained yet stained,
and being stained yet unstained," and so forth—
this is explained in terms of the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is called the ālayavijñāna,
and it coexists with ignorance and the seven consciousnesses."
"Like the waves of the great ocean,
they are constantly uninterrupted," and so forth;
it further says:
The Tathāgatagarbha,
when perfumed by beginningless false and evil habitual tendencies,
is called the "storehouse consciousness" (vijñānagarbha).
It is further said:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and it experiences suffering and pleasure."
It arises or ceases simultaneously with its causes,
just as a performer produces various musical performances and the like;
this is explained in detail in the two versions of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
These [distinctions] are all explained in terms of the gate of arising and ceasing.
However, these two gates are,
in their very essence, universally interfused.
Boundaries are undifferentiated;
essence and appearance are non-dual,
making them difficult to designate with names.
Therefore it is said, "The one mind has two gates," and so forth. Within the section on "Comprehensive Inclusion," there is first the establishment [of the gates] and then the explanation.

These two kinds of gates each comprehensively include all phenomena (*dharmas*). Regarding the statement that "each includes all phenomena": [This means that both gates, individually, encompass the entirety of reality.]
In the "Section on Establishing the Thesis" above, it simply says "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*);
however, in the current commentary, it says "each comprehends.
This is because the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*) is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of both the defiled and the pure.
Because there is no separate defilement or purity apart from their common characteristics,
they are subsumed collectively.
Just as fine dust is the universal characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of an earthen vessel—
apart from this universal characteristic there is no separate earthen vessel, and all earthen vessels are subsumed within fine dust—
so it is with the gate of True Suchness (tathatā-mukha).
One should know that it is likewise so;
it may be understood by analogy.
As for the "gate of arising and ceasing":
This is the specific characteristic of defilement and purity.
Phenomena with specific characteristics are subsumed under arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, because this True Suchness (tathatā) combines with conditions to transform into all phenomena (dharmas),
and since these phenomena possess no separate essence,
they are subsumed back into the gate of True Suchness.
By collecting fine dust and the like within a ceramic vessel,
these two aspects are simultaneously encompassed as non-dual; therefore,
it can be said that they constitute the one mind.
Question: Since these two gates are equally inclusive of one another,
why does the preceding section on the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) indicate only the essence of the Mahāyāna?
The aspects and functions are not manifested [in the gate of non-arising];
within the gate of arising and ceasing,
all three are fully manifested.
Answer: Suchness is the gate of subsuming appearances to reveal reality;
for while not destroying appearances, it simultaneously subsumes them.
Thus, it encompasses both arising and ceasing.
Because the characteristics are obliterated and no longer exist,
it merely demonstrates the essence (*tattva*).
Arising and ceasing constitute the gate of "gathering principle to form phenomena."
Because it accomplishes phenomena without destroying principle,
it encompasses True Suchness (tathatā);
because it accomplishes phenomena without losing principle, it is established.

It fully demonstrates the three great aspects. Answer: Because the essence is not established apart from characteristics; therefore, by demonstrating the characteristics, one simultaneously demonstrates the essence. Furthermore, because the essence is not separate from characteristics, if one were to demonstrate only the essence while omitting the characteristics, it would be like a person with cataracts seeing a flower in the sky—though the essence exists, it cannot be perceived. Thus, by demonstrating the characteristics, one simultaneously demonstrates the essence. Furthermore, one might attempt to grasp it through principle, yet because the principle does not exist [as a substantial entity], one should merely indicate its characteristics and functions.
Answer: This is not analogous.
Why is this? Because the arising of birth and cessation must necessarily rely upon the Truth;
by embracing the principle, the principle is not lost.
Because True Suchness does not necessarily depend upon arising and ceasing,
its characteristics are extinguished and do not persist. Because its characteristics are extinguished and do not persist, [it is thus].
It indicates only the essence because the principle is not lost;
it fully indicates all three.
Therefore, the meaning of "comprehension" (she) signifies equality, while the meaning of "manifestation" (shi) signifies distinction.
Below, the text investigates and explains to establish this point. It asks:
"What is the meaning of this? and then poses the challenge: "How so?"
If the two gates were separate,
they could not follow one another;
if the source is but a single mind, [they are inseparable].
It cannot be captured by a shadow,
because these two gates are not separate from one another. In the answer,
the phrase "not separate" is used because their essence and their characteristics are inseparable.
It is like gold and its ornaments:
if one gathers them back into the gold,
the ornaments leave nothing behind.
By means of the complete inclusion through the "Golden" [category], there is no gold that is not exhausted.
This is truly because these two gates are of one principle, their entirety encompassing all.
This principle is likewise so;
it may be seen by reflecting upon it. Second, regarding the detailed explanation, there are two parts:
first, the individual analysis of the two gates.
This reveals that movement and stillness are not identical.
Following the passage "Entering the Gate of True Suchness from the Gate of Arising and Ceasing," it clarifies the convergence of phenomena with reality.
This reveals that movement and stillness are not different.
Within the preceding section, the explanation of the two gates constitutes two parts.
First, regarding the gate of True Suchness (tathatā):
First, the heading;
second, the explanation.
Within the explanation, there are two parts.
First, it is stated that the essence is beyond words in order to clarify the object of contemplative wisdom;
this explains the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) from the preceding "Section on Establishing the Meaning."
Secondly, from the passage "Furthermore, as for True Suchness" (*tathatā*) onwards,
the qualities are distinguished based on verbal expression;
this clarifies the object of faith in order to explain the previously established characteristic of the Middle True Suchness.
The beginning and middle have two parts:
first, a general presentation of the essence of the dharma;
second, questions and answers that resolve doubts.
The initial text has two parts:
first, the direct revelation of the essence of suchness;
second, from "by all verbal expressions" onwards, the reconciliation of attachments and the explanation of the name.
The preceding section has three parts.
First is a brief indication according to the actual reality.
Next is the section beginning with "All dharmas."
The delusive is gathered to reveal the true.
Therefore, the following section concludes by showing that the true is free from the delusive.

The mind-as-suchness (cittatathatā) is precisely the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm. Regarding "the first, the single Dharma-realm" at the beginning:
it means that the non-dual true mind constitutes the single Dharma-realm.
This is not a matter of numerical calculation.
It is called "one" because it is, according to principle, empty, fused, equal, and non-dual.
Furthermore, because there are two meanings regarding the term "lower basis," it is here referred to as simply "one" in terms of its essential substance.
It is called the "Dharmadhātu" (Dharma-realm) because it gives rise to the dharmas of the noble ones.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states:
"The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is so called because it has the meaning of being the cause of the noble dharmas."
Therefore, it is called the "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu),
for the noble dharmas arise based upon this object;
herein lies the meaning of "cause."
This is because it refers to the meaning of "element" (dhātu).
Regarding the term "great general characteristic," among the two gates, one does not take up the gate of specific characteristics.
Within this, one grasps only the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*),
yet it also fully encompasses all particular characteristics;
therefore, it is called "Great" (*mahat*).
This single Dharma-realm,
in its entirety, constitutes the gate of arising and ceasing;
in its entirety, it also constitutes the gate of True Suchness.
To clarify this meaning, it is called "essence" (*tattva*).
That which serves as a guide to produce understanding is called "dharma.
That through which noble wisdom universally traverses is called a "gate" (*mukha*).
What is called "the nature of mind is neither born nor extinguished"? To say that the nature of mind is neither born nor extinguished is an explanation of the aforementioned essence of phenomena;
it means that [the nature of mind] does not arise in accordance with delusion.
It does not cease through the remedy;
furthermore, it does not arise through cultivation,
nor does it cease while remaining within defilement.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Because the mundane is not destroyed and the supramundane is not exhausted. (2) Regarding the second section, "Reconciling the False to Reveal the True," there are two points.
All dharmas exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought; if one is free from mental ideation, then there are no signs of any objective realms. The adherents say:
"We clearly perceive the differentiation and flux of all dharmas."
Why, then, is it said that the nature is without arising or ceasing?
The commentary states:
"As for the characteristics of differentiation..."
This is produced by your own pervasive conceptualization and deluded sentiments;
it has been fundamentally without reality,
just as one with diseased eyes falsely perceives flowers in the sky.
Therefore, it is said that they all have their distinctions based upon deluded thoughts.
A doubter further asks:
"By what means can it be known that they arise based on deluded thoughts?"
The commentary states:
Because the various sages are free from deluded thoughts,
such objects do not exist for them.
This proves that this object must certainly arise from delusion.
Furthermore, if this object were not a product of delusion and were truly existent,
the noble ones would not fail to perceive it.
It must be delusion;
since ordinary beings see it,
it must be awakening.
If one does not see flowers in the sky,
it must be due to diseased eyes;
apply this analogy in reverse.
Therefore it is said: "If one is free from thought, there is no inequality. (3) Regarding the eight phrases in the conclusion:

"For this reason, all dharmas, from the very beginning, are free from the mark of verbal expression, free from the mark of names, and free from the mark of mental objects; they are ultimately equal, without change or variation, indestructible, and are solely the One Mind, and are therefore called True Suchness. As for "for this reason":
Because that which is grasped is fundamentally empty,
and because the true mind is immovable,
all phenomena are therefore identical to True Suchness (tathatā).
That which is free from the characteristics of verbal expression does not exist within the sounds of speech;
it is free from names and designations.
Because it is not expressed through words and phrases,
these two lines transcend the path of language and are not the object of the wisdom derived from hearing.
That which is free from mental objects is not a conceptualization of mental discourse; thus,
the sphere of mental activity ceases.
It is not an object of the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Above, it was called "True" (*tattva*) because it is free from falsehood and delusion;
below, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*) because it is free from diverse characteristics (*vividha-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the last three phrases explain each other in succession,
[referring to] the objects of supramundane cultivated wisdom.
It is associated solely with correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
As for the term "ultimate equality," although it pervades both the defiled and the pure, it refers here to its association with correct wisdom.
This is because its nature is eternally non-dual.
The reason it attains this non-duality is that it remains unchanged from beginning to end while abiding within conditions.
It is said that there is no change or alteration.
The reason it attains non-alteration within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is that it does not share the nature of the conditioned, which is subject to destruction.
This means that while remaining within defilement, one is not destroyed;
the path of cultivation is not ruined.
It is solely this single mind.
Because it returns to and is identical with the essence of the Dharma, it is named "True Suchness" (*tathatā*).
This is the naming based on its meaning. Second, regarding the second assembly’s interpretation of the name through the perspective of grasping, there are two parts.
First the explanation, then the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are three parts.
First, the direct reconciliation of the adherence to [erroneous] views.
Second, from "Regarding verbal expression, it is extremely inferior" downwards, doubts are resolved by explaining in terms of names.
Third, from "The essence of this suchness" downwards, the [notions] are dispelled by explaining in terms of characteristics.

Because all verbal expressions are merely provisional names without reality and cannot be apprehended as they merely follow deluded thoughts, it is said that even "suchness" has no characteristics. Regarding the first part, the statement "Because all verbal expressions are merely provisional names without reality": [This means: All verbal expressions are merely provisional designations lacking substantial reality. They arise in accordance with deluded conceptualization and are ultimately unattainable; therefore, even that which is termed "suchness" is devoid of any defining characteristic.
It is stated that verbal teachings are not real and should not be grasped literally;
the phrase "but [they arise] following deluded thoughts" explains the reason why they lack reality.
I fear that ordinary and ignorant people, upon hearing the name "True Suchness" mentioned above,
might claim that the author’s own words are self-contradictory,
since the preceding text stated that it is "free from the characteristics of names."
For what reason, then, is this name "Suchness" established? Therefore,
the current explanation— which dispels [the notion that] conventional designations are not real—
is not contradictory.
Furthermore, when it is said that there is "no characteristic," it means the elimination of characteristics.
This is because names are established in dependence upon characteristics.
Because both are objects of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"Characteristics and names constantly follow one another, giving rise to various false imaginings (*vikalpa*)."
Therefore, both are now dispatched. II. Regarding the second section, the specific application of the names, there are two parts:
first, the delimitation of the names;
second, the intent behind establishing the names.
This refers to the ultimate limit of verbal expression, wherein words are used to dispel words. A doubt arises at the beginning:

"Since names and characteristics have been severed and only provisional, adventitious names are established, why is no other name established instead of exclusively using the term 'Tathatā' (Suchness)?"
The commentary states:
"Suchness (tathatā) is the ultimate limit of verbal expression."
That is to say, after this name,
there is no further name;
thus, among all names—
It is the ultimate limit; therefore,
among the ten names within the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
the name "Tathatā" (Suchness) is the tenth, the name of the final culmination.
Therefore, it is called "the ultimate.
As for the statement that words are used to dispel words,
this name "the ultimate" was established for that purpose.
It is for the purpose of dispelling names;
if these names did not exist,
there would be no means by which to dispel them.
If this name remains, one does not even dispel the name;
it is like striking a bell until the sound subsides.
If this sound did not exist, other sounds would not cease.
If one were to strike repeatedly to preserve this sound,
it would itself become a source of clamor.
Nor is it merely sound;
one should know that the underlying intention here is likewise so.
One must carefully discern this. [Section 3: A specific analysis of the characteristics in two phrases.]

The essence of this *tathatā* (suchness) has nothing that can be discarded, because all phenomena are entirely *tathatā*; nor does it have anything that can be established, because all phenomena are identical to *tathatā*. Regarding the statement that "the essence of this *tathatā* has nothing that can be discarded," etc.:
There are two interpretations.
The first, explaining by way of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), states:
"The opponent observes that the preceding text has simultaneously negated both the name and the characteristic of *tathatā*."
This means that if the essential nature of true suchness (tathatā) were also considered a phenomenon subject to negation,
one would give rise to the view of nihilism (ucchedadṛṣṭi).
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
It merely dispels false names and signs,
but does not dispel the true dharma of suchness;
for it contemplates the object by means of this sublime wisdom.
As for why they are not sent away,
the following sentence explains:
because all phenomena are entirely true.
There is no dharma that can be discarded.
When outsiders hear that true reality is not discarded,
they claim there must be some dharma that can be established.
Because one clings to emotional conditions,
it is said that "there is likewise nothing that can be established";
this is because one has departed from deluded emotions.
As for why it is not established,
the subsequent sentence provides the explanation;
this may be understood.
Second, the explanation according to the Dharma states:
"There is nothing to be discarded" does not mean that the true essence discards the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
As for why they were not sent,
the commentary explains:
it is because all phenomena are entirely true.
Because all phenomena of defilement and purity within the gate of arising and ceasing lack intrinsic nature and are not different from true suchness.
It does not depend on being dispelled,
nor is there anything that can be established;
for all phenomena such as arising and ceasing have never not been true.
This suchness does not depend on being established.
Why does it not depend on being established?
The following sentence explains:
Because all dharmas are identical to suchness;
because all dharmas of arising and ceasing, etc., are fundamentally identical to suchness;
this true suchness has never failed to manifest.
Furthermore, what else could be established?
Moreover, according to the two gates mentioned above,
each one respectively encompasses [the whole] in its entirety.
Regarding the phrase "all phenomena," four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established herein. First,
with respect to reality (*tattva*), there is nothing to be discarded.
Because the conventional is itself the ultimate;
secondly, regarding the ultimate, it does not depend on being established,
for the ultimate that is identical with the conventional is primordially manifest.
Third, regarding the conventional, there is no contradiction,
because the ultimate is identical to the conventional.
Fourth, regarding the conventional, it does not depend on being established.
Because it is the differentiation of the conventional within the ultimate,
for this reason,
the gate of arising and ceasing is not destroyed.
The gate of True Suchness is taught,
and the gate of Arising and Ceasing is taught without destroying the gate of True Suchness;
this is because these two gates are in fact but the one mind.
Therefore, the ultimate and the conventional are fused together without obstruction.

Consequently, objective spheres manifest as false appearances.
These two, along with the first, all reside within the state of the *ālayavijñāna* and belong to the category of non-associated mental factors (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The third is the characteristic of cognition.
This refers to the delusion regarding objects manifested by one's own mind due to ignorance,
whereby one falsely gives rise to the conceptualization of the characteristics of defilement and purity.
Therefore, it is called "wisdom.
Fourth is the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*),
which means that due to ignorance (*avidyā*), one does not comprehend that what was previously conceptualized is empty and non-existent.
Furthermore, the arising of thoughts continues in uninterrupted succession.
These two exist together at the stage of the subtle differentiation of the *vikaḷpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness),
belonging to the associated mind (*samprayukta-citta*).
Ignorance combines with the characteristics of the preceding life,
transforming that pure mind until this stage; at this point,
its mode of activity remains subtle.
The firm persistence of attachment to dharmas is called the characteristic of abiding;
it refers to the latter two among the three subtle states mentioned in the subsequent text.
Furthermore, these include the first two among the six coarse factors,
the last four among the five mental factors,
and the middle four among the six defilements.
These are all identical in being the characteristic of this abiding.
As for the two distinct characteristics,
the first is the characteristic of grasping.
Second is the characteristic of calculating names and words (*nāma-pada-lakṣaṇa*).
This refers to how this ignorance, deluded regarding the aforementioned phenomena of defilement and purity, as well as opposition and compliance,
further gives rise to greed, hatred, the view of a self and persons, and attachment.
Grasping at signs and calculating names leads to increasingly deep attachment;
this occurs at the stage of the coarse division of the phenomenal consciousness (*vṛtti-vijñāna*),
where ignorance is in conjunction with the preceding state of abiding.
It turns that pure mind toward this stage;
its mode of activity is somewhat coarse and agitated,
causing the body and speech to engage in the performance of karma.
This is termed "dissimilar characteristics" (visabhāga-lakṣaṇa).
Among the six gross factors (audārika) mentioned below, it corresponds to the middle two;
and among the six defilements (saṃkleśa), it corresponds to the first.
Together with the five consciousnesses and the subsequent mental consciousness,
these are all alike in their distinct characteristics.
As for the statement that "the characteristic of cessation is one":
This is called the characteristic of initiating karma.
It means that this ignorance does not understand that good and evil karmas will inevitably bring about the two retributions of suffering and pleasure;
therefore, it extensively encounters various conditions to construct and accumulate all manner of karma.
One experiences the fruits of karma according to one's actions;
by extinguishing the preceding divergent mind, one causes oneself to fall into the various realms of existence.
Through the power of ignorance, that pure mind is transformed.
Reaching this posterior limit,
the mode of activity is most coarse;
reaching this point, it is the ultimate.
The ultimate end of its exhaustion is called the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).
This is the fifth characteristic among the six gross characteristics mentioned in the subsequent text.
Because the fruit of retribution cannot be severed,
the sixth characteristic is not considered. Therefore,
the four characteristics within the three realms are nothing but the dream-mind.
All are due to the power of fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
Thus, a sutra says:
"The dwelling-place of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) possesses the greatest power."
This treatise states below:
"One should know that ignorance can give rise to all defiled phenomena.
This is what is meant.
Although one distinguishes the four characteristics according to their progression from the subtle to the manifest,
from beginning to end they ultimately have no sequence;
these four characteristics taken together constitute a single thought-moment.
Because the coarse and the subtle are fused into a single mind,
it is said that they exist simultaneously and none possess independent self-existence.
However, this has not yet exhausted the ultimate source.
According to the depth of one's practice, there is a perception of sequence; however,
for one who has reached the source of the mind,
the four phases of a single thought-moment are known simultaneously.
The Sūtra says:
"Bodhisattvas know the end but do not know the beginning;
only the Buddha-Tathāgata knows both the beginning and the end."
The "beginning" refers to the characteristic of arising;
the "end" refers to the remaining characteristics up to the characteristic of cessation.
Thus, by the power of the non-awakening of ignorance, various dream-like thoughts such as the characteristic of arising are produced.
The source of the mind is stirred, turning toward the state of cessation;
yet it has long slumbered within the three realms and wandered through the six destinies.
Now, by the power of the inconceivable perfuming of original enlightenment (*mūla-jñāna*), one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment and seeking.
Furthermore, as for the cause:
the teachings of hearing that flow from the true mind permeate the original enlightenment;
because their essence is identical and their functions are harmoniously integrated.
It takes up that perfuming by hearing,
increases the power of innate understanding,
and diminishes the capacity of ignorance.
Gradually approaching the source of the mind,
one first ceases the characteristic of extinction and finally ceases the characteristic of arising.
He attained great and clear awakening, realizing that the source of the mind is fundamentally unmoving;
it is quiescent from beginningless time,
equal and perfectly equal.
There is no difference between non-enlightenment and enlightenment, as illustrated in the sutras by such analogies as crossing a river in a dream;
the general meaning is as follows. Next, the commentary on the text is explained.
The four stages are distinguished by means of the four characteristics of the provisional entrustment (*āśraya*).
Within these four stages, there are four meanings each.
The first is the person who is capable of contemplation (*pratyavekṣaka-pudgala*).
Second, the characteristics of the object of observation;
third, the benefits of the observation;
fourth, the limits of the observation.

What is the meaning of this? It is like ordinary people who, because they perceive that an evil thought has arisen in the preceding moment, are able to restrain the subsequent thought so that it does not arise; yet although this is called "awakening," it is in fact non-awakening. This refers to the initial stage.
As for the "ordinary person," this refers to one capable of contemplation,
whose stage is that of the Ten Faiths.
"Being aware when a preceding thought gives rise to evil" clarifies the characteristics of what is observed;
this refers to the period prior to entering the ten stages of faith.
Having extensively created evil karma of body and speech without awareness,
one now enters the stage of faith and is able to know that such evil karma will certainly bring about the retribution of suffering.
Therefore, it is called "awakened awareness.
This clarifies the meaning of being aware of the characteristic of cessation.
That which is able to arrest subsequent thoughts so that they do not arise—
Discerning the benefits of contemplation:
Previously, due to a lack of awakening, one constantly gave rise to evil karma of body and speech;
now, because one has awakened, one is able to refrain from creating such evil.
"Cessation" refers to the characteristic of extinction.
Although it is termed "awakening," it is in fact "non-awakening";
this concludes the section on the limits of contemplation.
Being able to know that the characteristic of cessation is truly unwholesome,
one does not commit evil;
this is called "being awakened."
Yet they still do not know that the characteristic of cessation is a dream;
therefore, it is said that they are "unawakened.
This [state] is merely able to cease unwholesome karma.
Therefore it is said that although there is awakening,

hence it is called non-awakening.
Question: Since one does not perceive subsequent moments when perceiving distinct characteristics and so forth, why is the designation "non-perception" not also established for that?
Answer: If one bases it on the fact that one perceives what precedes and does not perceive what follows, it may indeed be termed "non-perception."
Therefore, the subsequent passages state that everything up to the tenth stage is non-awakening (*abodha*).
Even if one has attained awakening regarding karma but remains unawakened regarding afflictions (*kleśa*),
this is precisely what is termed "non-awakening."
This refers precisely to this passage.
It is because awakening and delusion are directly opposed to one another,
and not because of karma.

Just as the contemplative wisdom of the two vehicles and the initial resolve of bodhisattvas perceive that the thought and the difference in thought have no different characteristics, and because they abandon the coarse marks of conceptualization and attachment, it is called "similar awakening. In the second stage:
Those capable of observing persons are the Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages and those above the stage of Ten Understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*).
The initial mind of the Ten Understandings is called the Dwelling of Arousing the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*).
By citing this initial person, one includes all subsequent stages.
Therefore, it is said that they are those who have first resolved their minds and so forth.
Although these bodhisattvas do not realize the emptiness of persons because they intentionally retain their afflictions,
these bodhisattvas at this stage truly attain mastery over the emptiness of persons.
This is a discourse on the common stage with the Two Vehicles.
"Awakening to the difference in thought" refers to the characteristics that are the objects of observation.
As explained above, these two types of differentiated characteristics—the internal and external—consist of the conceit of "I" and "mine," greed, hatred, views, and attachment;
these are commonly understood by both types of persons.
The inherently pure mind is slumbering under ignorance;
it dreams of various phenomena and gives rise to all manner of afflictions.
Now, it gradually accords with wisdom.
Because one attains a slight awakening from a dream of differing characteristics,
it is said that "one awakens to the difference in thought.
As for observing the benefits:
Since one is already able to awaken from a dream of diverse appearances,
those diverse appearances dreamed of are forever non-existent; therefore,
it is said that "one contemplates the absence of diverse appearances."
Regarding "by abandoning coarse conceptual attachment to signs," this explains the characteristic of benefit.
Arising of desire, hatred, and so forth is termed "coarse conceptualization."
Attachment to favorable and unfavorable conditions is called the characteristic of clinging.
Because one awakens from dreams characterized by difference, one is able to abandon them;
yet one still remains asleep within the dream of abiding characteristics.
Therefore, it is called "similar cognition" (*sādṛśya-bodha*).
This concludes the section on the limits of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-pramāṇa*).
In this stage, the bodhisattva has not yet reached the stage of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-avasthā*).
Because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not fully comprehend the emptiness of phenomena, their realization is called "semblance awakening" (*sādṛśa-bodha*).

For instance, Bodhisattvas on the level of the Dharma-body awaken to the fact that mindfulness in the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is characterized by non-abiding; because they have abandoned the coarse characteristics of discursive thought, this is called "partial awakening" (*pradeśa-bodha*). This refers to the third stage.
Regarding those who are able to contemplate this:
Bodhisattvas of the first stage realize the meaning of the pervasive nature of the Dharmakāya,
and this realization continues identically through all stages up to the ninth stage.
All are called Dharma-body Bodhisattvas.
Regarding "awakening to the abiding of thought":
it means awakening to the characteristics of the four preceding types of abiding.
Although one knows that all phenomena are nothing but consciousness and thus does not give rise to coarse,
deluded attachments or conceptual discriminations regarding anything external to the mind,
nevertheless, after emerging from meditative observation:
Regarding the phenomena manifested within one's own mind,
one still gives rise to conceptual discrimination that clings to them as being either defiled or pure;
thus, that pure mind is dormant under the influence of ignorance.
The dream exists within the state of abiding;
now, it is conjoined with non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
One awakens from the dream of the state of abiding.
Reflecting back, one finds that the characteristic of abiding is ultimately non-existent;
therefore, it is said that "one awakens to the abiding of mindfulness, yet mindfulness has no characteristic of abiding.
This is because one is free from the characteristics of coarse conceptualization and discursive thought.
This clarifies the benefit [of the teaching]:
because it differs from the previous person’s grasping and attachment to external objects,
it now refers simply to "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) in relation to the mind.
Furthermore, because it differs from the subsequent fundamental ignorance in its subtle aspect of arising,
it is called the "aspect of coarse thought.
Among these four modes of abiding:
In the first, seventh, eighth, and ninth stages,
one is respectively free from one characteristic each;
this shall become clear in the text below.
Although one has attained awakening regarding the coarse characteristics of the foundations of mindfulness,
one still sleeps within the dream of the characteristics of birth; since the realization of the Path is not yet perfected,
it is said to be "partial."
This marks the conclusion of the section on contemplation. As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:

"When the stages of a bodhisattva are fully perfected through skillful means, the mind of awakening arises in a single thought-moment; yet this mind has no initial characteristic because it is far removed from even subtle thoughts. Thus one perceives the nature of the mind, which is eternally abiding—this is called ultimate awakening. This refers to the fourth stage.
"Exhausting the stages of the Bodhisattva" means that because the awakening of the ten stages has reached its ultimate limit, it is called "exhaustion.
This is a general statement.
The latter two phrases provide a specific clarification.
"The fulfillment of skillful means" refers to the path of skillful means.
"Correspondence in a single thought-moment" refers to...
This is the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
As stated in the Abhidharma-śāstra:
"The path of ultimate attainment (*niṣṭhā-mārga*)..."
This refers to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). It is of two kinds:
that which is subsumed under the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
And that which is subsumed within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*)— this is precisely the person who can contemplate herein.
Regarding the phrase "the initial arising of the awakening mind":
Raising up the object of contemplation:
"The mind first arises" clarifies that fundamental ignorance is deluded because it depends upon awakening.
The moving mind stirs the still mind to give rise to subtle thoughts;
now one realizes that apart from fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi), there is no non-awakening.
Thus, the moving mind is originally quiescent.
It is like one who is disoriented and mistakes the east for the west;
upon awakening, that which was the west is seen to be the east,
and no further appearance of "west" remains.
Therefore, it is said that the mind has no initial characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Although each of the preceding three stages possesses its own respective awakening, [the mind remains without an initial characteristic].
Because their movement of thought has not yet been exhausted,
they speak only of the non-abiding nature of thought and so forth; however,
this is within the stage of ultimate consummation.
All movements of thought are exhausted, and only the single mind remains;
therefore it is said that the mind has no initial characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
This refers to one who is free from subtle thoughts.
To clarify the benefits of contemplation:
the movement of the karmic consciousness within each moment is the most subtle;
it is termed "subtle mentation."
This refers to the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
Since this characteristic is entirely exhausted and remains forever without residue,
it is said to be "far removed" (*viveka*).
Because one is far removed from false appearances,
true nature is revealed;
thus it is said that one "sees the nature of the mind."
Within the first three stages,
because the characteristics are not yet exhausted, one does not speak of "seeing the nature.
In these preceding stages, awakening has not yet reached the source.
It is like a dream-image arising that moves that still mind,
causing the karmic consciousness and its associates to arise and cease without abiding;
now this arising-image of the dream has ended.
When the wind of ignorance ceases, the waves of the ocean of the mind subside;
it remains profoundly still and eternally abiding.
Therefore, it is said that one attains the vision of the nature of the mind, and that the mind is itself eternally abiding.
As for ultimate awakening:
previously, one had not yet reached the source of the mind;
dream-like thoughts were not yet exhausted.
Seeking to extinguish this agitation, I hoped to reach the other shore;
now that both dreams and thoughts have utterly ceased,
I have awakened to the source of the mind.
Fundamentally there is no transmigration;
now, quiescent from the beginningless past,
it is eternally and spontaneously one mind.
Equal and equal;
from the beginning not different from the source,
it is called ultimate awakening.
This marks the conclusion of the section. Second, the citation and explanation has four parts:

Thus, the Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings who can contemplate non-thought, they are then heading toward Buddha-wisdom. Regarding the initial statement that those who can contemplate non-thought head toward Buddha-wisdom:
While on the causal stage,
although one has not yet abandoned discursive thought,
one is able to contemplate such a principle of non-discursiveness.
It is said that this capacity for contemplation is directed toward Buddha-wisdom;
by this, one realizes that the stage of Buddhahood (buddhabhūmi) is free from discursive thought (an-asmṛti).
This is a statement made by citing the cause with reference to the fruit.
If one explains this by citing its established position,
as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:
"Based on the various paths of subduing, the mind that gives rise to phenomena ceases."
The path of abandonment according to the Dharma extinguishes [afflictions] by means of the fundamental mind;
the path of supreme extraction exhausts the fundamental mind.
This refers to all paths of suppression.
This refers to the three stages of the ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Regarding the cessation of the mind that engages with phenomena:
it is precisely the relinquishing of coarse conceptualization and attachment to signs within this treatise.
This is the cessation of distinct characteristics.
As for the path that severs phenomena,
it resides in the stage of the Dharma-body.
Regarding "extinguishing based on the fundamental mind":
this refers to the extinction of the characteristic of abiding, which occurs when one abandons the coarse characteristics of discursive thought within this treatise.
The path that excels and uproots is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
That which exhausts the fundamental mind is...
In this treatise, as it is said, "to be free from subtle recollection" means that the characteristic of arising has been exhausted.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "as for the arising of the mind," there is no initial characteristic that can be known; yet, to speak of knowing an initial characteristic is precisely what is meant by non-recollection (*amanasikāra*). In the "Re-explanation," it says: "Furthermore, as for the arising of the mind."
This reiterates the previous statement regarding the initial arising of the awakened mind;
it does not mean that during the time of awakening one perceives an initial characteristic.
Therefore, it says there is no beginning that can be known.
Since there is no initial characteristic (*ādi-lakṣaṇa*),
why is it said that one knows the initial characteristic?
The explanation states:
To speak of "knowing the beginning" refers precisely to non-thought (amanasikāra),
which is like being aware of the present moment.
To know the west is itself the east;
there is no further characteristic of "west" that can be known.
As for the statement "knowing the west":
This refers precisely to the East.
When awakening the mind,
one knows that the very first stirring of thought is inherently still.
Therefore, it is said that this is precisely non-thought (*amanasikāra*).

For this reason, all sentient beings are not called awakened, because from the very beginning their thoughts have continued in succession, never having been separated from thought; thus, it is called "beginningless ignorance" (*anādikālikāvidyā*). Regarding the phrase "for this reason" (*tasmāt*) within the discussion of the failure [to awaken]: [Note: The provided text contains a partial commentary on the term *tasmāt* (is hence/therefore) as it appears in the context of explaining why sentient beings fail to attain awakening.]
This is because the prior absence of thought is called awakening;
it thus reveals that the presence of thought cannot be called awakening.
Regarding the phrase "from the very beginning," etc.:
This reveals the reason for non-awakening:
all sentient beings from the stage of the *vajra* downward have not yet abandoned the thoughts of beginningless ignorance;
therefore, they do not receive the name of "awakened."
Thus, while it was previously stated that awakening occurs gradually due to the distinctions between the four phases of a dream,
it is now said that there is no awakening because of the lack of distinction within the sleep of ignorance (*avidyā-nidrā*).
As the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) states:
From the initial stage of the Patience of Submissiveness up to the Samādhi of the Summit,
one illuminates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
yet this is not termed "seeing."
That which is called "the seer" refers to this very omniscience (sarvajñā).
This is what is meant.
Thus, the statement regarding "beginningless ignorance" establishes the meaning of non-awakening (*abodha*).
This demonstrates that there is no defiled phenomenon (*saṃkliṣṭadharma*) that begins with ignorance.
Therefore, it is said to be "without beginning.
Furthermore, because ignorance relies upon the Truth (Tathatā),
they share the same lack of an original beginning.

If one attains non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*), one knows that the characteristics of the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the mind are equalized through non-conceptualization. This explains the attainment of the Middle Way.

If one reaches the source of the mind and attains non-conceptualization, one then universally knows the distinctions between the four characteristics of the single mind as it moves and transforms within all sentient beings.
Therefore, it is said that if one attains non-conceptualization (amanasikāra), one then knows the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the mind.
The phrase "because of [the equality of] non-conceptualization and so forth" explains and establishes the preceding meaning.
A doubt arises:
"The Buddha has attained non-thought,
whereas sentient beings possess thought."
Existence and non-existence are vastly separated;
how can one know [the latter] through [the former]?
The commentary says:
Sentient beings possess thought;
fundamentally, they are without thought.
Since the Buddha has already attained that state of no-thought, [he is thus called the Buddha].
Non-thought and thought are fundamentally equal;
therefore, it is said that "because non-thought is equal [to thought]," by which one comes to understand this.
Another explanation states:
because within each of the four modes of mindfulness there is precisely non-mindfulness,
it is said that "by means of non-mindfulness," and so forth.
Therefore, one who attains non-thought thoroughly knows the mindfulness of the four marks.
From here below, it clarifies that the beginning is not different from the fundamental;
herein, first there is the heading, followed by the explanation.

In reality, there is no distinction between initial enlightenment (shijue), for the four marks exist simultaneously and all lack independent existence; they are fundamentally equal and identical to a single awakening. Thus, although one initially attains the awakening of non-thought, it is [identical to that original state].
However, the four marks that are awakened to are fundamentally without arising;
in dependence upon what non-awakening could there be the distinction of "initial awakening"?
This explains the meaning stated above by showing that the four marks occur simultaneously.
These four characteristics are formed by a single mind;
they are linked like a chain in continuous succession without before or after,
and apart from this pure mind, they have no separate intrinsic nature.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are from the beginning equal and identical within the single primordial enlightenment (*ādibuddha*).
Nevertheless, until this stage is reached,
awakening occurs according to the capacity of one's wisdom, proceeding through successive stages.
Because they had not yet conformed to the Dharma, they could not be identical to the original;
now that the four characteristics are simultaneous and equal,
one realizes that all lack intrinsic nature.
Since it is this same single original enlightenment (abhisambodhi), there is no distinction between original and initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi).
Question: How can the four marks [of existence] be simultaneous?
Since they occur simultaneously,
why does the preceding passage state that there is a sequence between the two awakenings?
The answer has already been established above.
This means that within a single dreaming mind, the four characteristics flow in succession;
those who are in the dream perceive them as preceding and succeeding moments,
each according to the depth or shallowness of their own cognitive power.
One perceives these [dreams] as distinct parts;

however, one who possesses great awakening knows that the four characteristics of the dream are but a single pure mind, devoid of any substantial nature that can be distinguished as preceding or succeeding.
Therefore, it is said that they do not exist simultaneously with any independent self-existence, and so forth.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"In a dream, one may think years have passed,
yet upon awakening, it is but a brief moment."
Therefore, although time is immeasurable,
it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa.
Herein, "one kṣaṇa" refers to:
This refers to non-thought.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"All phenomena are unborn."
I speak of the meaning of the moment:
that which is born immediately ceases.
This is not taught for the sake of the ignorant.
The commentary states:
Because that which flows and transforms moment by moment necessarily lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
and because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is precisely non-arising (*anutpāda*).
If there were not non-arising, there would be no cyclic flow.
Therefore, it is only those who realize non-arising who perceive the momentary.
Furthermore, in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra:
"Neither arising nor ceasing is the meaning of impermanence," and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra* states:
"The seven consciousnesses do not undergo transmigration, nor do they experience suffering or pleasure."
It is not the cause of nirvāṇa.
The tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure,
and is accompanied by their causes.
Whether arising or ceasing—
these scriptural passages all clarify that the true mind follows along with the flow to produce defiled and pure phenomena;
these defiled and pure phenomena fundamentally lack intrinsic nature.
Because there is no intrinsic nature, there is only the single true mind.
Therefore, the four phases are identical to the single true mind;
non-awakening is itself identical to original awakening.
Therefore, it is said that they are fundamentally equal and identical in their single awakening.
